extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, students, and researchers preparing citations in Chicago style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating Chicago-style citations for periodicals (journals, magazines, newspapers), websites, blogs, social media, interviews, and related items, including special cases (supplements, special issues, electronic supplements) and formatting/punctuation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOI placement and punctuation for electronic sources
rubrics_metrics.description: When DOIs or other identifiers are included for electronically published sources, they should immediately precede the URL (or database information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separated from the surrounding citation by commas in a note and periods in a bibliography entry. Example: narr & krist ... 81, accessed August 1, 2017, https://doi.org/10.1086/679411.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page-number punctuation relative to volume/issue
rubrics_metrics.description: When page numbers immediately follow a volume number, separated only by a colon (as in a shortened citation), no space follows the colon. But when parenthetical information intervenes, a space follows the colon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to other types of volumes as well. Examples: Social Networks 14:213-29 (no space after colon); Critical Inquiry 1, no. 3 (Winter 1975): 479-96 (space after colon because parenthetical intervenes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comma (not colon) when page follows issue number
rubrics_metrics.description: When, as occasionally happens, the page number follows an issue number, a comma—not a colon—should be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Diogenes, no. 25, 84-117.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation format for journal special issues
rubrics_metrics.description: A journal issue devoted to a single theme is a special issue; it carries normal volume and issue numbers and may have an editor and a title of its own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An article within the issue is cited as a normal article; the special issue as a whole may be cited as: Tomii, Reiko, and Midori Yoshimoto, eds. “Collectivism in Twentieth-Century Japanese Art.” Special issue, Positions: Asia Critique 21, no. 2 (Spring 2013).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation format for journal supplements
rubrics_metrics.description: A journal supplement is numbered separately from the regular issues of the journal and may have its own title and author or editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate supplement and its number (e.g., Supplement, Signs and Society 3, no. S1 (2015): S174-94) and include DOI if available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles published in installments
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles published in parts over two or more issues may be listed separately or in the same entry, depending on whether the part or the whole is cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite parts individually if only a part is used (e.g., pt. 1, pt. 2) or combine entries if citing the whole (show both volume/issue and page ranges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing versions appearing in multiple publications
rubrics_metrics.description: When a chapter or article has appeared in more than one form (journal, later in book, etc.), cite the version actually consulted in a note or text citation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If of interest to readers, add annotation about the previous or alternate version following the citation (e.g., 'Previously published as “Article Title,” Journal Title 20, no. 3 (2016): 345-62').

rubrics_metrics.name: Add place of publication for ambiguous journals
rubrics_metrics.description: If a journal might be confused with another with a similar title, or if it might not be known to users of a bibliography, add the name of the place or institution where it is published in parentheses after the journal title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Lost in Thought: Undergraduate Research Journal (Indiana University South Bend); Victorian Poetry (West Virginia University).

rubrics_metrics.name: Translated or edited article citation follows book rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A translated or edited article follows essentially the same style as a translated or edited book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include translator or editor elements analogous to book citation examples (e.g., 'trans. Tim Z. Translator' or 'Edited by Edward A. Editor').

rubrics_metrics.name: New series identification in journal volumes
rubrics_metrics.description: New series in journal volumes are identified by n.s. (new series), 2nd ser., and so forth, as they are for books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note the comma between the series identifier and the volume number. Example: Proceedings of the Massachusetts Historical Society, 2nd ser., 10 (January 1896): 414.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short titles for subsequent article references
rubrics_metrics.description: In subsequent references to journal articles, the author’s last name and the main title of the article (often shortened) are most commonly used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the absence of a full bibliography, the journal title, volume number, and page number(s) may be more helpful. If page numbering is not continuous by volume, include the issue number in the short form (e.g., '63 (2): 225').

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstracts treated like journal articles
rubrics_metrics.description: An abstract is treated like a journal article, but the word 'Abstract' must be added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Matute, Daniel R. '...'. Abstract. American Naturalist 185, no. 2 (February 2015): 253-69.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing electronic supplements or enhancements
rubrics_metrics.description: Components of journal articles with a printed counterpart that are offered only online (supplementary data, supporting information, enhancements) can usually be cited according to how they are referred to in the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate file formats for multimedia content if relevant; include table/figure labels or dataset file names and DOIs or repository links where applicable. See examples for MP3 audio, online-only tables, and Dryad deposits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic citation format for magazine articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of magazine articles are capitalized headline-style, set in roman, and placed in quotation marks; magazine titles are in italics and an initial 'The' is usually dropped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weekly or monthly magazines are usually cited by date only (date not in parentheses); inclusive page numbers may be omitted; when page numbers are included, a comma separates them from the date. Examples provided (Cornell Alumni Magazine, New Yorker).

rubrics_metrics.name: Magazine articles consulted online
rubrics_metrics.description: For magazine articles consulted online, include a URL at the end of a citation or, if no suitable URL is available, the name of the database.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific page numbers usually will not be available but may be cited if they are. If article is delivered via an app, cite the app or device name in parentheses (e.g., New Yorker (iPhone app)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting magazine departments and untitled departments
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of regular departments in a magazine are capitalized headline-style but not put in quotation marks; a department without a named author is best cited by the title of the magazine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Talk of the Town, New Yorker, April 27, 2015'; 'Gourmet. Kitchen Notebook. May 2000.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic citation format for newspaper articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Author (if known) and headline or column heading are cited like magazine elements; month, day, and year are indispensable. Page numbers are usually omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because newspapers may have multiple editions/sections, include edition identifier or section if useful; for online articles include URL or database name. Example entries and guidance to include final edition, section number, or city edition when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite time stamps for frequently updated news items
rubrics_metrics.description: Because news sites may update certain stories as they unfold, it may be appropriate to include a time stamp for an article that includes one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List the time as posted with the article; if the time zone is not included, determine from context. Retain a copy of the article as cited (see 14.15). Example includes time and 'EST'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper headlines in citations: headline-style capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: In source citations, Chicago recommends headline style for citing headlines in notes and bibliographies for consistency with other titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headlines presented entirely in full capitals in the original are usually converted to upper- and lowercase in a citation (with some exceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles of newspapers: omit initial 'The' and add location if needed
rubrics_metrics.description: An initial 'The' is omitted from the title of a newspaper; a city name (or state/province) may be added in parentheses after the title if the title does not include it and identification is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-known national papers (Wall Street Journal, Christian Science Monitor) do not require city names. For papers published in other nations, a nation identifier may be used (e.g., Times (UK)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular columns, features, editorials, letters formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular columns or features may carry headlines and column titles; these should appear in roman, capitalized but without quotation marks. Editorials may be described generically; letters to the editor are usually treated generically without headlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples showing how to cite columns, editorials, and letters; readers’ comments are treated like blog comments (see blog guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsigned newspaper articles and reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Unsigned newspaper articles or features are best dealt with in text or notes; if a bibliography entry is needed, the title of the newspaper stands in place of the author and the item is listed under the periodical's title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show listing under newspaper title and/or using the article headline in the note.

rubrics_metrics.name: News services and news releases citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of news services (Associated Press, UPI) are capitalized but not italicized; a news release is treated similarly to a news article and should include release number and date when available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Federal Emergency Management Agency, 'FEMA Awards...' news release no. RV-NR-2015-006, March 19, 2015, https://...

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation elements and order for reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: In citations of reviews include: (1) name of reviewer if signed; (2) title of the review, if any; (3) the words 'review of' followed by the work reviewed and its author; (4) location and date for performances; (5) the periodical listing in which the review appeared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a review appears in a bibliography, alphabetize by the reviewer's name or by the periodical title if unsigned. Examples for book reviews and performance reviews provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: website, blog, social media
rubrics_metrics.description: Website refers to a collection of web pages at a specific location; a blog is a web-based forum of posted entries organized by date or topic; social media refers to internet-based forums for public communication on platforms or services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories overlap; a website can host blogs or social media content, and all can include multimedia. Social media can be private and then cited as personal communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles formatting for websites, blogs, and social media
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of websites are generally set in roman without quotation marks and capitalized headline-style. Titled sections/pages of a website are usually placed in quotation marks. Blog titles can usually be set in italics; blog posts in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A website analogous to a printed work but never printed (e.g., Wikipedia) can be treated as a website (roman) rather than a conventional encyclopedia. When in doubt, opt for roman. Many sites have no titles—cite the responsible entity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing web pages and websites: required elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To cite original website content include as much of the following as can be determined: title or description of the specific page; title/description of the site as a whole; owner or sponsor of the site; and a URL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add the word 'website' (or 'web page') in parentheses if the nature of the source may otherwise be unclear. Include publication date or date of revision/modification; if none, include an access date. For frequently updated resources include a time stamp.

rubrics_metrics.name: If site content changes or ceases to exist, note and retain copy
rubrics_metrics.description: If a site ceases to exist before publication, or if the information cited is modified or deleted, this information should be included in the text or note; authors should retain a copy of any source that is likely to change or disappear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dates and URLs can help readers find the information via the Internet Archive; examples show citing a discontinued site and note about removed projection text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing blog posts and whole blogs
rubrics_metrics.description: Blog posts are cited like online newspaper articles: author of the post; the title of the post in quotation marks; the title of the blog in italics; the date of the post; and a URL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word 'blog' may be added in parentheses after the title of the blog. Blogs that are part of a larger publication should include the publication name. If citing the entire blog, list it under the editor (if any) or the title of the blog in a bibliography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing comments on posts
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments can usually be cited in the text, in reference to the related post. If cited in a note, list the name of the commenter and the date of the comment, followed by information for the related post.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a shortened form to refer to a post fully cited elsewhere; a URL for the comment is usually unnecessary but may be listed if available. For obviously fictitious names, no need to add 'pseud.'; names in all lowercase can usually be capitalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing social media content: five-element structure
rubrics_metrics.description: For social media content include: (1) the author (real name, if known, followed by screen name in parentheses; if only screen name is known, use it); (2) in place of a title, the text of the post (quote up to first 160 characters); (3) the type of post (service and description, e.g., Twitter, Instagram photo); (4) the date (month, day, year; time stamps usually unnecessary); (5) a URL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the post has been quoted in the text it need not be repeated in a note. Time stamps may be included to differentiate posts on same day. Comments are cited in reference to the related post. Frequently cited accounts or extensive threads may be included in a bibliography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain copies of social media content
rubrics_metrics.description: Because social media content is subject to editing and deletion, authors are advised to retain a copy of anything they cite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 14.15 for guidance on retaining copies; examples provided for tweets, Facebook posts, Instagram photos, and comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing electronic mailing lists and forums
rubrics_metrics.description: Content posted to electronic mailing lists or forums can be cited like other social media: include name of correspondent, title/subject of thread (in quotation marks), title of list/forum (followed by 'list' or 'forum' if not part of title), host site title, date of message, and URL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posts on private forums or lists can be cited like personal communications (see 14.214). Examples: mailing list archive entries and Quora replies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpublished interviews citation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Unpublished interviews are best cited in text or notes; citations should include names of person interviewed and interviewer, brief identifying info if appropriate, place or date of the interview (or both), and where a transcript or recording may be found if available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permission to quote may be needed; examples show formats for in-discussion citations and archived interview transcripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing unattributed or confidential interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: An interview with a person who prefers to remain anonymous or whose name should be withheld may be cited in whatever form is appropriate in context, with explanation of the absence of a name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an explanatory note such as 'All interviews were conducted in confidentiality, and the names of interviewees are withheld by mutual agreement.' Example: Interview with health-care worker, July 31, 2017.

rubrics_metrics.name: Published or broadcast interviews citation
rubrics_metrics.description: An interview that has been published or broadcast or made available online can usually be treated like an article or other item in a periodical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include URL if consulted online. Examples include Paris Review interviews, PBS broadcasts, and Charlie Rose interviews with links where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal communications handled in text or notes
rubrics_metrics.description: References to conversations (face-to-face or by telephone), letters, email or text messages, or direct/private social media messages received by the author are usually run into the text or given in a note and are rarely listed in a bibliography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most such information can be referred to simply as a conversation, message, or the like; the medium may be mentioned if relevant. Examples: 'In a conversation with the author on January 6, 2009...' and short note examples for email and direct messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit personal email addresses from citations
rubrics_metrics.description: An email address or the like belonging to an individual should be omitted from citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inclusion is necessary in a specific context, it must be cited only with the permission of its owner. See related chapter on permissions (13.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of quoted social media text in notes vs. text
rubrics_metrics.description: If the post has been quoted in the text, it need not be repeated in a note.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Otherwise include the text (up to 160 characters) in place of a title in the note, per social media citation rules.
